The Struggle to Recover from Catastrophic Loss: A 3 Year Old's Response to the Early Death of Her Mother

Annette Mendelsohn

Annette Mendelsohn

Pond Street
London NW3 2QG

Annette Mendelsohn  

Introduction

This paper is a presentation of my work with Rachel, a three year old girl whom I saw four times weekly for two and a half years at an outpatient hospital clinic. The work presented covers the first two years of therapy.

Rachel was brought for assessment by her father and step-mother because of increasing alarm over her behaviour at home. She was described as being agitated, tense and aggressively demanding. During the day she had repeated periods of screaming when she avoided physical holding or comfort. At night her sleep was also disturbed by frequent screaming tantrums.

History

Three months following Rachel's birth, her mother was diagnosed as having breast cancer. The on-set and subsequent progression of the disease was rapid and she died when Rachel was fourteen months old. Following their mother's death, Rachel and her older brother were looked after by a live-in nanny until their father re-married a year later. Rachel's difficulties began to surface following her father's marriage to her stepmother and escalated during the pregnancy and subsequent birth of a new baby.

Initial Assessment

I first met Rachel in the waiting room where she had come with her stepmother for her first session. She was reluctant to come with me at first, but soon took my hand and walked quietly with me to the consulting room. Inside the room she stopped still next to my chair, looked around and chewed her fingers. Then she began to look at me and we continued to look at each other for some moments. I felt an immediate liking for her. She stood smiling at me and after what seemed a fairly long exchange of looking at each other I began to speak to her about the toys prepared in a box for her to use whenever she came to see me, who I was and the times of our sessions together. I told her that her mummy and daddy had told me about some of the worries they thought she had been having recently and that her play with me in the therapy room could perhaps help her to sort out some of her worries. As I spoke, Rachel continued to stare wide-eyed at me, showing no interest in anything apart from my face and saying nothing in response. After a short pause I began to wonder aloud about the strangeness of the room and of me and that she might not feel sure of me or of what I might do.

A Child Losing and Finding Her Objects: An Unusual Therapeutic Intervention in the Nursery School**

Jill Miller

Jill Miller

Denver

Jill Miller  

Carmen, a healthy, attractive child, began attending the Centre's Nursery School when she was 3 years old. The family was well known to the staff, who were aware that Carmen had not lived with her mother for some time. The family had made a trip abroad to relatives when Carmen was 15 months of age and had abruptly left her there, in the care of an aunt. The reason given was that only two plane reservations were available, too few to include Carmen. Her mother planned to collect her three months later, but did not make the trip. When Carmen was 23 months she was visited by her mother with the idea of returning to England, but her mother again left without her. Twenty months after being left the first time, at the age of 3, the mother visited again. This time she brought Carmen back to England with her. Once here Carmen cried each night at bedtime: “I want to go home”. She soon began to call her mother “Mummy”, but continued to call her aunt “Mummy” as well. Two weeks afer her arrival Carmen entered our Nursery School.

We were later to learn that these were not the only dramatic separations between mother and child. The details were unclear; however sometime during Carmen's first year she lived with her aunt in another country for six months. Until the time of entry into the Nursery, it seems Carmen had lived with her mother for only 9 months of her life, during which she saw her mother on weekends, being cared for during the week by someone else.

When Carmen entered the Nursery she was like a whirlwind and settled poorly. The staff drew a picture of an exhausting and exasperating child who grabbed what she wanted from everyone, pushed and pulled, hit, kicked, scratched and bit other children, knocked over chairs or threw things in anger, gathered and lost toys, and was into everything and everyone's belongings. She screamed and wailed without provocation and laughed in a falsetto way. She countered any attempt to talk to her about her losses and what had happened to her by hitting out at the questioner's face. Observers termed her “wild and uncivilized”.

Johannes Bodtker, the author of Beyond Words practises as a Child Psychiatrist in Oslo, Norway. In his book he describes his work with children in short term psychotherapy using interpretive art therapy as a means of enabling these children to reach unconscious processes more readily. His book is based on five case studies, accompanied by an introduction which provides a theoretical background to his work. This is based on a psychoanalytic model adhering to the basic principles of Freud and Klein.

He uses Freud's understanding of the interpretation of dreams to explain the way in which art activity incorporates the mechanisms of displacement and condensation which become embodied within the symbolic content of an art work. This notion is coupled with the idea that through spontaneous visual expression and with the aid of sublimation, the child using art in this way creates the ability to express pre-conscious and unconscious thoughts and feelings. Bodtker incorporates Freud's ideas on sublimation together with Kleinian object relations theory which he employs in his analysis and interpretation of these visual images. In this process he involves himself with the image making process as a whole, which would include the way in which a child paints and draws and how, for example, he might physically use his art materials.

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson

35 Crooked Usage
London N3 3EU

Judith Jackson  

In this paper I shall attempt to describe and discuss some initial consultations with a two year old boy and his parents who were referred to a child guidance clinic when all other medical interventions failed to deal with the child's incessant screaming. Christopher was described as a child who had been screaming virtually from birth. The Paediatric Registrar at the time wrote to the Consultant Psychiatrist saying that she was surprised that his mother had not battered this child long ago. At the time of the referral he was on strong tranquillising and sleeping drugs and had even been hospitalised for a week when a year old in order to investigate organic causes - probably too, to offer some relief to his distraught and persecuted parents.

Very little was understood about the origins of the screaming and how ultimately a stop could be made. Medical investigations and various suggestions about techniques of managing the situation had very little impact. When I undertook to see Christopher and his parents I was very open as to how I would proceed with the exploration of the problem(s).

First Consultation

Unfortunately the first meeting was arranged on a day of torrential rain, so they arrived three quarters of an hour late. Christopher appeared then to me as a large, pale, strained looking two year old, with small beady blue eyes, stocky but uncertain posture and a whiny and irritable manner, probably exacerbated by the long wet uncomfortable journey. His parents looked very strained as well as drenched, so the session began with their apologies to me for their late arrival and mine to them for not being able to see them for very long, because I knew well the conditions that had delayed them. Time taken for unbuttoning coats and depositing bags seemed a necessary practical prelude to opening up to the problems with which they had come. We made a triangle with the parents on the two large armchairs and myself in the desk chair.

Christopher immediately made for the box of assorted toys and teddy I had placed on the floor in the centre. He took the teddy bear and placed it on a chair away from us and then started exploring the box, taking out the two large elephants and the cars. I was surprised that he seemed able to explore freely. He placed the large elephant on a truck and when it toppled over he abandoned that and picked up the mother doll and the little girl doll. Mother made “isn't it pretty” sort of noises about the doll, without actually knowing, I felt, what she was saying, I was acutely aware of her depression and sense of exhaustion.

Interiority and Creativity: the Therapy of an Art Student**

Lynda Miller

Lynda Miller

112a Nelson Road
London N8 9RN

Lynda Miller  

Introduction

In this paper I attempt to explore developments in the inner world of an art student in intensive therapy, and to suggest how this corresponds with the unfolding of creative processes. At the beginning of the therapy the patient, whom I shall call Tessa, was 22 years old, and she complained of being hardly able to work creatively at all.

My intention is to try to make some links between development of the therapeutic process in terms of the transference relationship, changes in Tessa's art work as she described them to me, and a progression shown in phantasies and dreams. From an overall perspective this could be understood as Tessa's gradual emergence from a dark, furtive and intrusive way of being into a world of colour and space and of relationship to others.

Assessment

In the first assessment interview Tessa told me that she had been to the clinic before, when she was 6 years old, following her parents’ divorce. It was thought then that Tessa was depressed, and she described to me how she would refuse to get out of her sleeping bag. She went on to tell me that she had hated her first therapist, and continued as follows relating her childhood memories of therapy, with rather pointed reference to her present experience with me:

With feeling, she described this dark, ominous gloomy building; she was been in a very narrow, dark room (she quickly glanced around the room we were in)… Every time she picked up a toy the therapist said something ‘significant’ (Tessa's tone of voice very mocking) so she didn't touch the toys, farmyard animals, as they were all ‘significant’; she brought he own from home next time.

My first impression of Tessa was that she looked much younger than her twenty-two years. I was struck by her rather childlike and serious demeanour, which was accentuated by her slight build, short straight hair-style, and plain dark-coloured clothes. She had referred herself to the Clinic ostensibly because she felt worried that she was unable to do any work at Art college, having, in her words, “rubbished it” in her mind.

Margot Waddell  

In Britain the clinical community - unlike the academic and feminist/intellectual - has maintained a rather xenophobic insularity in relation to French theoretical developments of the last few decades. The domination, perhaps more apparent than real, of French intellectual life by structuralism in general, and Lacanism in particular, has posed a barrier of conceptual inaccessibility for those brought up within a more empirical tradition - with all its attendant prejudices. The tendency has been to keep away from ‘foreign’, especially French, ideas, with only a few exceptions, the work of Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel and André Green, for example.

To this somewhat myopic attitude recent translations of the work of Didier Anzieu and his colleagues offer a welcome antidote, consisting as it does of a thoroughly comprehensible model of a psychoanalytic approach to the self rooted in the earliest psychic development of the infant. The ideas have important implications for work with severely disturbed, autistic and psychotic children, enriching and extending our current and still limited understanding of this troubling area. As such they complement and contribute new dimensions to theories conceptually familiar within the British tradition, yet cast in a distinctively different form, and in some ways much more extensively elaborated than their English counterparts.

This body of writing is characterised by the very absence of dogmatism, by breadth and range of thought as well as depth, and by the way in which the central concepts are developed out of a commitment to look both inward and outward simultaneously, and to examine the interface between. Anzieu positions himself thus in the opening pages of The Skin Ego:

“There is an internal conflict in psychoanalytic thinking between an empiricist, pragmatic, psychogenetic orientation (more common among the British and Americans), in which the psychical organisation is seen as resulting from unconscious childhood experiences (particularly of object relations), and a structuralist organisation (dominant in France in recent decades) which denies that the structure is a product of experience, affirming on the contrary that there is no experience that is not organised by a preexistent structure” (1989, p. 4).

Alison Cantle

Alison Cantle

Alison Cantle  

Joy Schaverien is an experienced teacher and practitioner of art therapy who has long been interested in the nature of transference and countertransference in art therapy. This book is an investigation of these phenomena from a theoretical point of view which Schaverien often claims is a new one. Her aim is “to establish the central role of the picture as a vessel within which transformation may take place and this involves the picture as an object of transference”. Schaverien's main influences are Jung and the philosopher Emst Cassirer. It is from these two sources that she derives the term “analytical art psychotherapy” to describe a form of art therapy where the picture is understood to be “an object of transference and countertransference itself with implications for the wider therapeutic relationship”.

Schaverien proposes that there are two different, although linked, transferences within the art therapeutic relationship, one to the therapist and one to the picture. It is this other transference which forms one of the main themes of this book and which Schaverien names the “scapegoat transference”. This biblical scapegoat, she explains, was ceremoniously embodied with the sins of the community before being cast out into the wilderness to die leaving the community purged. Schaverien argues that this offers a useful way of understanding the engagement of the patient with art objects made in therapy. “Like the scapegoat”, she writes, “the picture may be experienced as a embodiment, and so its disposal may play a significant part in the resolution of the transference”. I remain unconvinced by Schaverien's idea of a second transference and think her concept of the art object as a scapegoat could be adequately explained by psychoanalytic theory. However, the notion of what she refers to as “disposal” raises some interesting issues when considering the real differences between art therapy and psychoanalytical psychotherapy.

The Group Setting

This paper describes a group which took place over a four year period on an eight-bedded adolescent surgical ward in a small children's hospital. The patients comprised mainly severely disabled adolescents, with conditions such as spina bifida, hydrocephalus and nephrotic syndrome, a number with complex orthopaedic problems who were less disabled, some with primary enuresis and encopresis, some general accident and emergency cases, a few psychiatric admissions and a number for specialist dental care. The age range was from thirteen to eighteen years, though many of the spina bifida patients were older, some as old as twenty three. The ward was served by a number of consultants to cover the different specialisms involved. There was a ward sister, three or four qualified nurses, and a large turnover of nurses in training and junior medical staff. A number of other professional and ancillary staff had contact with the ward. The ward had a diffuse set of systems of responsibility and power, and generally it fell to the ward sister to provide some cohesion.

A weekly group for the patients had been started three years before by the Consultant Child Psychiatrist as a response to increasing demand from ward staff for emotional help (not necessarily psychiatric intervention) for adolescents on the ward. It was initially formed then as a response to the presented multivariety of individual patients’ needs. Lead usually by a child psychiatrist and a teacher, the aim was to encourage the patients to express their feelings in the group and appreciate together common concerns. New staff extended the aim to include offering patients help to gain more psychological understanding of their medical conditions. I was asked to take over the group as a complex going concern with the same teacher who had been there all along when the child psychiatrist left for another post.

The ward group met weekly at a specified early afternoon time and it lasted an hour. We spent about three quarters of an hour before this on the ward, getting an update on patients from the staff and talking to the patients and their parents about the group. After the group we would spend another half an hour talking with the staff involved in the group about the themes that day.

This book gathers together the papers of Mrs Dockar-Drysdale which are not already to be found in her two previous publications Therapy in Child Care (1968) and Consultations in Child Care (1973). These volumes have been out of print for some time, although her present publishers have indicated an intention of reprinting them as companions to the new volume.

The book contains twenty-two chapters of varying length. Some are texts of papers given at Conferences in the UK. Others are brief essays of a few paragraphs concentrating on problem topics which perhaps arose in the course of her work as Therapeutic Consultant, the role she fulfilled for twelve years at the Mulberry Bush School before transferring to the Cotswold Community twenty years ago.

The papers bear a strongly individual stamp which reflects the personality of their author. Mrs Dockar-Drysdale produces quite contrasting reactions, with listeners and readers, ranging from admiration to outright dismissal. I suspect this book may produce similarly diverse reactions.

Editorial

This issue marks the end of my term as editor of the Journal. The editorship will be taken on jointly by Marianne Parsons and Anne Home.

I have greatly enjoyed my editorship and will miss the Journal very much; starting as a board member and then as editor, the Journal has been part of my life for a good many years.

Sad though I am to be leaving, I have every confidence in the new editors, and look forward to seeing the Journal enter a new dynamic phase under their skilled leadership.

This issue is a generic one, with four excellent accounts of individual treatments and two fine papers on applied work, one on an under-fives counselling case and another on a complex piece of adolescent group work. In addition we have some distinguished review essays on important recent books that are virtually articles in themselves. With so many stories of horrific residential child care practice emerging in the press these days, it can well be said that the publication of this book is timely. It is clear that residential practitioners, working in such everyday proximity with distressed and disturbed children, need to be more than adequately trained, managed, and supervised. It is equally clear that they and their managers need time and space to think and reflect on what they are doing - and that this can best be done in consultation with an outsider whose perspective is fresh and different from what may prevail within their establishments.

This book is about such consultation. It is a collection of chapters written by six consultants and two consultees describing their experiences in nine different residential establishments. The style and focus of the consultants is very varied; so too the work of the residential establishments. There is no question that the art of consultation takes many forms, as idiosyncratic as the consultants and the consultees who take part in it and as varied as the establishments and cultures in which it takes place. However, despite this rich mixture, the book managed to gather together the essential aims and functions of consultation and offer some very good theoretical understanding of what lies behind these different approaches. Some of its contributors provide remarkably honest accounts of their experiences which give the reader the opportunity to identify with and understand the human difficulty and uncertainty of it all.

London

Nancy Brenner  

Introduction - The Anna Freud Centre Nursery

The Anna Freud Centre Nursery School functions today much as it has since its beginning in 1957, its purpose being to provide the students training at the Centre with the opportunity to observe and study normal child development. It is attended by 13 children, who reflect the multicultural population at large. The age range is 2½ to 5 years. Most children are referred by health visitors or social workers because of a need in their families. There are always one or two children with special needs within the group.

Ongoing observations on the children are recorded daily by the staff; these observations help both staff and students to understand and learn more about young children. The first year students in training at the Centre observe in the Nursery School and meet in a seminar each week to discuss their observations. The Nursery Consultant leads these seminars. In addition, there is a weekly Education Unit Meeting with members of the Centre's staff and students at which a developmental report on an individual child based on the recorded observations is presented and discussed. Anna Freud's developmental viewpoint informs and underlies the work of the Nursery School.

The Usefulness of Recording Nursery Observations

Anna Freud introduced recorded observations in 1937 as part of the work of the Jackson Nursery in Vienna. In her paper for the 30th birthday celebrations of the Anna Freud Centre Nursery, Hansi Kennedy (1988) quoted from a lecture given by Anna Freud in 1966:

The Jackson Nursery was an experimental nursery for children between 1 and 2 years of age… the most underprivileged children that could be found in Vienna… This was an excellent opportunity for us to learn and to test out some of our theoretical ideas in an active plan of day care.

Hansi Kennedy went on to describe one of the monthly seminars set up to discuss the theoretical issues arising from the work in the Jackson Nursery (1 March, 1937).

Amongst other things they discussed was the methodology of data collection. Should one make behaviouristic observation, i.e. try to cut out all thoughts and impressions from one's mind and note down everything the child is going to do in a given time-span, or should one use what Anna Freud called “the analytic method?” She illustrated this by citing one child in the group whose masturbation problems revealed themselves very soon. Should the observations be centred on this impression, i.e. should observers gather material which confirms or contradicts this first impression?

This is an extremely helpful book and is a valuable addition to the literature available to those who find themselves working in this area. Its strength is as a reference book and arises out of the author's long and painful struggle to think about and work effectively in the field of child sexual abuse. It offers an understanding of sexual abuse, why it happens and what perpetuates it despite the abuser's avowed wish for it to cease (syndrome of secrecy and addiction). It also suggests helpful ways to proceed when a case emerges, as a disclosure or in the midst of interventions for other reasons. The author uses many diagrams and coins terms and phrases that explain processes and events and makes them memorable in a way that is very useful. Of particular interest are chapters 6 and 7 which consider the primary therapeutic intervention when the possibility of sexual abuse emerges, and chapter 12: treatment issues; but the whole of the second part of the book, “Practical Problems”, is worth consulting.

There are a number of issues the author emphasises that I think are important and worthy of note. He is clear about the “trusted person” to whom the child speaks who, he points out, is thereafter a significant figure that the child may well have chosen with care. This trusted person must be helped to accept their important role for the child. Others subsequently involved with the case need to give this serious consideration. His clarity about the role of different disciplines is important for us all, what we can do and what we cannot do. Those of us in mental health, and our colleagues in social services and the legal system, need this constant reminder. What I now call an anonymous consultation he calls an Anonymous Diagnostic Interprofessional Consultation. I have found this enormously helpful as a concept and in practice when it is unclear as to what needs to be done. It helps generate questions such as am I over-involved and too anxious or not anxious enough? It also gives an example of the author's capacity to generate phrases that encapsulate an idea.

Heierstuveien 3B

Anne-Marie Auestad  

Introduction

In this paper I intend to describe 4 year old Peter and his adoptive family in their struggle to function together as a family unit.

We (the two therapists - Anne-Marie Auestad and Anne Svestad - in the following text called AMA and AS) met Peter and his adoptive parents two years after the arrival in his new home in Norway, and were introduced to Peter's difficulties in attaching to his new mother. Peter seemed unable to integrate his past and present lives, showing us a self-sufficient facade, whilst striving to hide his needy, frustrated and furious infant self. In an attempt to cope with his previous separation experiences, he rejected his new mother, completely assigning all caring functions to his father, thus splitting his inner and outer objects into “good” and “bad”.

We were able to observe how unexpressed fantasies and emotions in the child and the parents had created vicious circles blocking nurturing interaction between mother and child.

Our main task was to develop communication and integration. As all family members suffered from feeling cut off in different ways and on different levels of experience, our aim was to bring them together.

We therefore felt it important to work in a family context. Within the family sessions, Peter was invited to express himself with toys and words. An intense process developed, in which Peter wholeheartedly displayed his emotions and fantasies, assigning the role of the rejecting biological mother to the author (AMA) who interpreted his symbolic play activity, in the attempt to bring past and present together.

It seemed essential to involve the parents in this process. In the present paper our aim is to illustrate the advantages of this particular way of working.

In the discussion I also intend to compare our clinical material with other descriptions of problems with adopted children and their families.

The Literature

The literature conveys growing interest in the problems of adoptive children and their families. Marshal D Schechter in his article, Psychoanalytical theory as it relates to adoption (1967), points to disagreements as to the question of the significance of adoption in the aetiology of pathology. He points to many factors possibly contributing to psychological problems such as: experience of early separations; multiple placements, and the fact that the child discovers adoption late and feels deceived.

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3

Juliet Hopkins  

Introduction

Infant-parent psychotherapy has developed to meet the needs of families in which the referred patient is an infant or toddler. It is a form of therapy which will appeal to an increasing number of child psychotherapists who find themselves expanding their work with parents and family groups. Currently the method enjoys the support of WAIPAD (the World Association for Infant Psychiatry and Allied Disciplines) and so has international appeal. Much of its psychodynamic approach is already familiar to members of our profession, who may discover that they have unknowingly been doing it already. However, a particular advantage of this therapy lies in the simplicity and clarity with which its essential principles have been formulated. This advantage both facilitates our communication with other professions and our participation in an international development.

Infant-parent psychotherapy was first described and named by Selma Fraiberg ten years ago in her brilliant book Clinical Studies in Infant Mental Health (1980). Since then significant clinical and theoretical contributions to the subject have been made by Bertrand Cramer and Daniel Stern (Cramer, 1986, 1987; Cramer and Stern, 1988), but in the UK we are only just starting to take advantage of these exciting developments. This paper aims to arouse interest in the method by describing and illustrating it, before briefly addressing the question of how we can encourage its use more widely.

Infant-parent psychotherapy relies on the assumption that there is no such thing as individual psychopathology in infancy. This does not mean that babies do not contribute individual difficulties from their side of the relationship. It does mean that symptoms in the infant can best be treated by treating the infant-parent relationship, rather than by treating either infant or parent separately. Like all short-term therapies, infant-parent psychotherapy is focused, and the focus is on the development of the infant who is always present in the sessions. The infant's presence ensures that parental feelings towards him are readily available in the here-and-now for exploration and interpretation. Interpretation, as practised by Selma Fraiberg, utilised a combination of object-relations and attachment theory to understand the ways in which the parental past interfered with relating to the baby in the present. The symptomatic infant was found to be the victim of negative transference, haunted by “ghosts in the nursery”. The primary focus of the work was on understanding the parents’ transference to their baby, rather than on understanding their transference to the therapist.

Editorial

This issue is the second of our “Special Editions” devoted to a specific theme - this time on work with children under five. Submissions to the Journal for this issue revealed the impressive extent and effectiveness of work being done with this age-group, particularly in the form of short term interventions with parents and infants, usually at an early stage in the development of difficulties. It would appear that, while individual psychotherapy is still the treatment of choice for some children under five, particularly in the latter half of the age range, many psychotherapists have been adapting their observational skills, insight and technique to a style of work with very young children and their parents that addresses the relationship between them directly.

Over and again, examples were given of cases where a mere handful of joint sessions made a profound and lasting impact on what had seemed to be overwhelming problems. In the interests of producing a balanced and representative Journal, it has not been possible to include all these fascinating papers, many of which illustrated a similar approach, but the first three published here give an idea of the nature and value of this kind of work.

The next two papers in this issue illustrate longer term treatments, but again in the first of the two the decision was made to conduct the therapeutic sessions with the parents present. The second is the only account in this Journal of a more “orthodox” individual psychotherapy. It might be felt that such treatment is under-represented in this issue, and indeed it was interesting that relatively few papers of this kind were submitted to the editorial board. What shines through all the papers, however, is that, although child psychotherapists are using their training and experience to respond flexibly to the needs of this youngest age group, their ability to do so rests solidly on the foundations of the deep understanding gained in individual work, coupled with the infant observation that is so essential a part of the initial training.

Marianne Parsons  

Introduction

This paper was written some years ago (1987), and therefore does not draw on the important work concerning the therapy of adopted children that was published subsequently, much of it in this journal (Hodges, 1989; Muller, 1989; Parsons, 1989; Salo, 1989; Green, 1990). I would also like to draw attention to the papers which arose largely out of the research in the Anna Freud Centre Study Group on Adoption (Berger, 1979, 1980; Berger and Hodges, 1982; Hodges, 1984, 1989; Hodges, Bolletti, Salo and Oldeschulte, 1985). This Study Group, set up by Maria Berger in 1978, explored two fundamental questions which adopted children have to face in their development, namely “Who were my first parents, what were they like?” and “Why did they give me up?” (Hodges, 1989). The Study Group also focused on the typical fantasies and theories of adopted children (Berger, 1979; Hodges, 1984), many of which preoccupied my patient, Sally. Jill Hodges (1989) referred to the universality of such fantasies in adopted children as a particular form of the family romance fantasy of the latency-aged non-adopted child. Sally's contradictory self- and object-representations were interwoven in her adoption fantasies, especially her view of herself as an unwanted child, and more specifically an unwanted girl.

At the core of Sally's problem was an inability to reconcile her intensely ambivalent feelings towards her parents, especially her adoptive mother. Her disturbance in self-esteem regulation was related in part to guilt and shame for aggressive wishes towards her adoptive mother, but was compounded by the mother's ambivalence towards her. Hostility towards her mother was so intense and unmanageable that Sally resorted to strenuous defence activity, including denial, repression and splitting of ambivalence. In the early stages of therapy this took the form of denying painful affects and conflicts, keeping knowledge of her adoption out of conscious awareness, and perceiving the adoptive mother as good and to be loved and the therapist (and later the biological mother) as bad and to be hated. A pattern emerged of uncontained excitement and sexualized anxiety in the sessions when Sally's wild physical and verbal expression of sadistic masturbatory fantasies were invariably triggered by material showing her wish for but fear of closeness with the therapist.

Marguerite Reid  

Introduction

“The fundamental difference between normal mourning on the one hand, and abnormal mourning and manic depressive states on the other, is this: the manic-depressive and the person who fails in the work of mourning, though their defences differ widely from each other, have this in common, that they have been unable in early childhood to establish their internal ‘good’ objects and to feel secure in their inner world. They have never really overcome the depressive position” (Klein, 1940, p. 369).

Within this paper I have considered my work with a six year old boy, whose mother, prior to his birth, failed to mourn the loss of a baby in a cot death. Klein suggested a link between failed mourning and an inability to “really overcome the infantile depressive position”. If a mother has been unable to establish an internal “good” object and has herself been unable to mourn, the question arises as to how this will affect her subsequent mothering and in particular her ability to help her baby negotiate loss and work through the depressive position.

Bion (1962) highlights the mother's role in containing persecutory anxiety through a state of “reverie”. He thought that as emotional states, both painful and pleasurable, were experienced concretely by the infant, the mother's ability to accept and digest emotional experience was essential for mental growth and ego development.

Isaacs-Elmhirst (1980) describes this when she writes:

“A normal baby's capacity to tolerate frustration is very small. When a normal neonate experiences frustration it is in a terrible state of suffering, which feels endless to the infant. This sense of urgency that an infinite agony must be stopped right away is projected into the mother. She must often, and normally can, react both appropriately and speedily. Reverie or alpha function can occur almost immediately” (p. 87).

The ability of a mother to help her infant face loss, both in his internal and external world, may be severely impaired if she has been unable to accept and digest her own experiences concerning loss. An unmetabolised experience of death may result in the infant's projected fear of dying arousing such psychic pain in the mother that she becomes unable to receive his projections. The uncontained projection, forced back into the baby as “nameless dread”, (Bion, 1962) increases his persecutory anxiety.

Introduction

In his poem The Little Girl Lost, William Blake describes the experience of the lonely Lyca who has become separated from her parents, and has “wandered long”. She says:

“Sweet sleep come to me

Underneath this tree

Do father, mother weep?

Where can Lyca sleep.

Lost in desert wild

Is your little child

How can Lyca sleep

If her mother weep?”

from: Songs of Experience, 1792.

The poem continues with Lyca being rescued by a “kingly lion” who keeps her safe with the other animals until her parents are guided to her. As in most of Blake's Songs of Innocence and Experience, the theme concerns the contrasting states of the human condition from blissful, happy innocence to the most painful and disillusioning impact of environment and the demands of growing up and taking one's place in society. These thoughts provide a backcloth to my work with a four year old whereby it became apparent throughout the twenty-one months of psychotherapy that she had experienced a very real loss of parental preoccupation; this had prompted her to turn to her own body products as a way of holding onto her object and maintaining a form of psychic equilibrium, as well as providing a means of controlling those affects aroused by the lost object, principally sadness and anger. Obviously, this had serious consequences both for her emotional development and her object relationships.

What Shall I Do to Stop Him Crying? Psychoanalytic Thinking about the Treatment of Excessively Crying Infants and their Mothers/Parents

Stella Acquarone

Stella Acquarone

27b Frognal
London NW3

Stella Acquarone  

Introduction

The simple question in the title, usually asked in a despairing way, evokes diverse and complex answers.

Excessively crying infants are approximately 10% of the infant population as described by Wolke and Gray (1989) and St James-Roberts (1989), and 10% is also the figure given in the longitudinal study made in New York by Thomas (1977). For newborns and 7-week-old infants who show temperamental difficulty by fussing and crying during the day, Wolke and St James-Roberts (1987) conclude that there is only low to moderate agreement between multi-method measurements and therefore no commonly identifiable “difficult” infant in the early weeks of life. Conversely, infants with “colic” syndrome have been identified in 26% of all cases as quoted by St James-Roberts (1989) in 21% described by Illingworth (1954) and 30% by Torup (1952).

In my clinical practice with cases referred for infant/parent difficulties, 45 out of 452 cases have been referred for crying alone, and 91 for crying mixed with other complaints, such as feeding and sleeping.

Clearly there are other disturbances of crying behaviour in infancy that are clinically important. It is interesting to note that in my general clinical practice the four most disturbed children that I treated showed an absence of crying behaviour in infancy and then in treatment cried in a way that was unrelated to what was actually happening in the session. In this paper, however, I am concentrating on children referred at least in part for excessive crying.

Aim of This Study

This is a retrospective analysis of all the cases of excessive crying that I have seen. Firstly I consider specific individual characteristics and secondly extrapolate general points to bear in mind when treating cases of this nature. I shall examine briefly the circumstances of the individuals who interact at the beginning of the problem, namely mother, baby and father, to see whether these follow certain patterns. I shall also examine the characteristics of psychodynamic treatment and ask whether there are any technical or theoretical aspects to consider.

Victoria Hamilton PHD

Victoria Hamilton

Victoria Hamilton  

To my knowledge, Sunday's Child is the first longitudinal study of the development of a child, filmed from the perspective of a child psychotherapist trained in the art and method of Infant Observation. Lynn Barnett's background in anthropology undoubtedly contributed to the innovative approach she has taken to the study of infancy since we are able to observe the intimate details of the baby's (Sunday's Child) daily life within his natural environment - first born child of professional parents living in a rural setting in the South of England. The opening shots of the first tape of the 8-part series (Part I, 0-3 months) show us the narrow streets surrounding the baby's home and we hear the voiceovers of his parents describing their expectations of their soon-to-be-born son. Throughout, the film-maker's commentary is kept to a minimum, thereby ensuring that observers share the experience of an anthropologist and/or trainee child psychotherapist entering unmapped territory with few signposts. To my mind, the film's greatest value results from the exposure to the ‘raw data’, specifically the raw emotions, of infancy and parenthood. Unlike other ‘developmental’ films, we are not presented with excerpts which have been selected in order to demonstrate the film-maker's thesis concerning aspects of normal - or abnormal - development. For this reason, the films are often hard to watch, particularly during the early days and weeks after the baby's birth when the relentless chain of events of feeding, changing, bathing, etc reveal the emotional field in which this child will develop.

As it is impossible to do justice to all of Lynn Barnett's films in one review, I shall assume that the majority of the readers of this review have had some exposure to Barnett's work over the last few years. I shall not, therefore, give an account of the films but rather review them from the point of view of their use as a teaching tool. I shall focus on the package of 8 films which cover the first 2 years of the baby's life (Sunday's Child: the Development of Individuality from Birth to Two Years of Age). Each of the 8 tapes spans a 3-month period and can be obtained separately.

Betty Joseph has been a practising psychoanalyst for fifty years. She shows, in this chronologically ordered series of papers, how she has developed an increasingly more careful process of getting to know, rather than know about, her patients. She has moved from writing about her patients “acting out” in the transference (Chapter 5) to “acting in” (Chapters 8,10,12) as though these were relatively isolated instances of unusual activity, to being attentive to all the moment-to-moment shifts and changes in the constant to and fro of living psychic change (Chapter 14). She now follows not only the patient's transference to her, and her counter-transference to them, but the effect of her counter-transference and her interpretation on them, and this is very much her own contribution, in spite of her debt to Klein and Bion. A natural modesty and a great respect for experience in all its imperfections and complexities means that she is never in love with an interpretation and also morally incapable of thinking in theoretical headlines. She refuses to carve the patient's experience up into oversimplified pieces, yet the writing is clear and convincing. The great weight of Joseph's work is to develop and expand Bion's concept of containment of the patient's projective identifications; she also pursues, however, some of its previously unrecognized implications.

Georgia O'Keeffe said that she decided to paint her flower canvases on a huge scale because in the hectic and technologically excited mood of New York in the 1920′s, no-one would look at small flower paintings, however exquisite. She decided that if she could paint the flowers big like the huge buildings going up, people would have to look at them.”- and”, O'Keeffe said, “-they did.” joseph is of a very different cast of mind; she simply asks people to look more closely at the flower - and, judging by the inspiring effect of her teaching worldwide, they do.

The thoughtful and clear General Introduction by the editors, Feldman and Spillius, lists four main theses: 1) Psychic equilibrium, (implied in which is the technical [and I would add theoretical] importance of exploration and description rather than explanation); 2) psychic change; 3) acting out or in the transference; 4) experiencing in instead of knowing about. The Relation of Infant Observation to Clinical Practice in an under Fives Counselling Service**

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller

120 Belsize Lane
London NW3

Lisa Miller  

In this paper I shall try to present some thoughts on the use of observation in a certain kind of psychoanalytically-oriented work. I shall do so by giving an account of a method of working and a service developed in the Child and Family Department at the Tavistock Clinic.

First, I need to describe the service offered in the Child and Family Department under the title “The Under Fives’ Counselling Service”. We offer brief help — only up to five sessions, which may be variously spaced out over a number of weeks — to families whose concern is focused on anxiety about their baby or small child. For example, we have mothers and fathers with babies who will not sleep, who will not eat, who cry incessantly; we have couples where the mother is depressed; we have parents anxious about the effects of bereavement or divorce; we have babies who refuse to be weaned, toddlers who suffer tantrums and jealousies; and of course we have those who come with more nameless and inexplicable anxieties. This service differs from the rest of the provision made in the Department insofar as here we do not regard ourselves as having a referred patient. We have parents coming for counselling; they come to think with an experienced outsider about the problems they perceive in their child or their children. The worker comes from a multi-disciplinary workshop where psychiatrists, social workers, psychologists and child psychotherapists meet regularly to discuss some of these cases and other aspects of work with very small children.

Flexibility, promptness and informality characterise the service. We see family members in various groupings: we like to see both parents, but we are quite willing to take what comes. We pride ourselves on being able to give an appointment quickly, sometimes very quickly, believing that in a case where anxiety involves a baby or small child help is needed now and can be used at once. The relative informality of the service means that self-referrals predominate. A mere telephone call secures a session. Certainly the parents need to have decided that they have a problem and it requires some courage to pick up the telephone and to come. But beyond that we try to put as few obstacles as possible in people's paths.

If I had to decide which was the central concept in Segal's thinking in this book I would say work - as in psychic work, dream work, working through. Working through psychic conflicts is not only part of the process of analysis but a fundamental function of the healthy mind. In this conception, both dreams and works of art are produced as part of a process in which basic conflicts in the personality - essentially the conflict of love and hate, of the wish to know as against the wish not to know, as well as the movement towards growth in conflict with tendencies to remain the same or to regress - are constantly being struggled with and reworked in the mind. There is not such a thing as arriving at a psychologically mature position and sticking to it; conflict is always present. This view of mental functioning derives from Freud's Formulations on the two principles of mental functioning (1911), from his theory of the life and a death instinct and from Klein's further elaboration of his theories in her own conceptualisation of the paranoid-schizoid and the depressive positions.

In this book Segal's original ideas, both those first published in two now classical papers On aesthetics, (1952) and On symbolism (1957), and on dreams (about which she wrote and taught extensively, and used profusely to inform all her work) are developed and integrated. The different chapters relate to the themes in the title, but these in fact interweave in the book. Dreams are used throughout, clearly and imaginatively, so one feels that however complicated the concept being explained, one has always a ‘picture’ as an illustration. In this way, other complex concepts which are fundamental for her thinking are also integrated and clarified - as Bion's theory of thinking, his concept of container and contained and also the difficult and often misunderstood concept of projective identification. She does not discuss technique explicitly (with the exception of the interpretation of dreams not primarily used for communication), but sometimes it is possible to read between the lines on technical issues; for example, some clinical examples make it clear that she uses reconstruction in analysis, and makes direct reference to the patient's past experience as such and she does not formulate her interpretations only in terms of the ‘here and now’.
